Mechanistically, foundation models exhibit a compute asymmetry: Evo2 40B frontloads compute into massive parameter scale to resolve single-nucleotide variants within a narrow 425-bp context window, whereas the bidirectional NTv3 650M model and the Genos 10B mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture backload compute to inference, requiring spatial logit aggregation and vast context windows of up to 94 kb. Furthermore, accuracy may benefit from locus-specific thresholding rather than mutation-class calibration, exposing representation boundaries of the self-supervised models.

items.title: SMFnet reveals principles of combinatorial transcription factor assembly
items.abstract_or_text: Combinatorial assembly of transcription factors (TFs) opens chromatin at cis-regulatory elements (cREs) to establish cell-type-specific gene expression. Dissecting the role of individual TFs and their collective function has been limited by the diversity of TF binding-site arrangements across cREs. A single regulatory sequence can support multiple configurations of TF and nucleosome occupancy, raising the possibility that distinct chromatin states reflect different TF assemblies. Predictive models linking regulatory sequence to chromatin accessibility collapse these distinct molecular states into population averages, obscuring how TF assemblies shape accessible chromatin. Here, we introduce SMFNet, a generative diffusion model that predicts distributions of single-molecule chromatin accessibility profiles from DNA sequence, and PRISM, which identifies sequence features associated with individual molecular states. Together, these approaches enable us to systematically associate single molecule chromatin states at cREs with specific TF binding motifs. Experimental perturbation of these motifs redistributes the corresponding states as predicted by SMFNet, supporting their interpretation as TF-dependent configurations underlying chromatin opening. We then use controlled in silico motif screens to systematically dissect individual and combinatorial TF contributions to chromatin opening. Individual TFs show distinct chromatin-opening signatures, differing in accessible-region width and nucleosome-positioning precision even when associated with similar levels of chromatin accessibility. Combining motifs reveals partner- and spacing-dependent effects on chromatin accessibility, TF occupancy and nucleosome positioning. Genetic perturbation of TF binding sites using natural variation at endogenous cRE confirms that TF-specific properties shape chromatin accessibility in vivo. Together, our findings reveal sequence-encoded principles of combinatorial TF assembly during chromatin opening.

items.title: IOP-independent treatment for neurodegeneration in glaucoma using optimized ROS-scavenging microparticles for sustained release of erythropoietin
items.abstract_or_text: Glaucoma is a slow-progressing neurodegenerative disease of the optic projection to the brain and a leading cause of blindness worldwide. Current treatments are targeted towards lowering intraocular pressure (IOP), the only known, modifiable risk factor; however, this strategy is ineffective in many patients. An early hallmark of glaucomatous neurodegeneration is increased reactive oxygen species (ROS), representing an alternative opportunity for intervention to halt or slow disease progression. In this work, we optimize a ROS-scavenging copolymer, poly(propylene sulfide-co-ethylene sulfide) (PPSES), for formulation of size-controlled, stabilized, antioxidant microparticles (MPs) for sustained release of the protein erythropoietin (EPO). EPO promotes biological antioxidant defense via activation of NRF2-mediated transcription of antioxidant genes. This MP system overcomes the short half-life of EPO and leverages the combined benefits of bioactive EPO with long-lasting, inherently antioxidant PPSES MPs. The lead EPO-MP formulation preserves neurons in both mouse and non-human primate models of glaucoma through suppression of oxidative stress and optic nerve degeneration. EPO-loaded PPSES MPs represent a translationally relevant therapy for long-term management of glaucoma independent of IOP.

items.title: ProtoPure: Literature Mining and Analysis of Protein Purification Protocols at Proteome Scale
items.abstract_or_text: Protein purification is a fundamental step for analyzing individual proteins and protein complexes and identifying interactions with other proteins, DNA, or RNA. A variety of protein purification strategies exist to address desired scale, throughput, and downstream applications. However, selecting an effective experimental procedure remains a largely empirical process that a quick literature review can help guide. Researchers typically survey on the order of a dozen publications for proteins with similar biochemical properties, assessing conditions on a case-by-case basis, leaving no systematic framework for comparison and decision-making at the scale of entire protein families. As protein engineering and design evolve, identifying effective purification conditions remains critical for obtaining sufficient quantities of properly folded and functional proteins. To address this gap, we developed ProtoPure, an LLM-based workflow and database that automates the extraction, standardization and analysis of protein purification conditions from peer-reviewed literature at scale. Given a user-defined UniProt table-enabling flexible selection of proteins by family, organism, or proteome. ProtoPure retrieves associated publications, classifies them based on the presence of purification protocols, and extracts a standardized set of 12 purification parameters (e.g., buffer composition, elution conditions). By transforming dispersed experimental descriptions into a structured resource, ProtoPure makes it possible to compare purification strategies across thousands of proteins. The resulting dataset revealed quantitative convergence toward a limited set of recombinant expression practices, with BL21(DE3)-based systems dominating protein production and recurrent combinations of expression host, inducer, growth medium, and plasmid occurring substantially more frequently than expected by chance. In contrast, downstream purification parameters exhibited greater diversity, revealing a workflow architecture that combines standardized expression infrastructure with more flexible biochemical components.

items.title: Mantpy: a framework for extracellular matrix analysis in spatial proteomics
items.abstract_or_text: Spatial proteomics technologies now profile cells and the extracellular matrix (ECM) together in situ. Yet analysis tools remain cell-centric, despite the ECM playing an essential role in health and disease. Here we present Mantpy, a framework that represents the ECM, and its interface with cells, as spatial graphs. Mantpy builds ECM graphs directly from matrix markers and links them with cell graphs for joint cell-ECM analysis, supporting graph statistics, explainable graph deep learning and visualisation. Mantpy extends from a single ECM marker to multiplexed cell-ECM panels. It recovers layered tissue architecture in the intestine from collagen IV alone, quantifies infection-associated ECM remodelling in mouse liver, and relates cells to the surrounding matrix in mouse lung, where cellular context recovers synthetically corrupted matrix labels. Released with ECM-inclusive datasets and interoperating with the scverse ecosystem and pytorch geometric.

items.title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake
items.abstract_or_text: In psychiatric practice, the clinical intake interview remains a primary diagnostic instrument, requiring the clinician to establish rapport while disentangling complex, overlapping presentations. Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study (N = 60 matched scenario pairs, 120 encounters) comparing the RL-trained agent against its identically prompted base model, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients while a separate panel of 15 independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored the de-identified transcripts. The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs (p < 0.0001), with gains on an adapted clinical-examination rubric (d_z = 0.77, p < 0.0001), patient-centered communication (82.0% vs. 65.2%, p < 0.001), and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%, p < 0.001). Across 127 psychiatrist-validated simulated intake scenarios, the trained agent nearly doubled its base model's clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294, p < 0.0001). To systematically probe conversational safety, we established two Delphi-consensus taxonomies, of clinical safety risks and relational competencies, from which 256 challenging adversarial presentations were derived; we find that training in simulation environments more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks (12.9% vs. 30.5%, p < 0.0001). Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters, though residual gaps require safeguards and clinician oversight.

items.title: MutQA: A Cross-Validated Q&A Dataset for Genetic Mutations
items.abstract_or_text: We introduce MutQA, a dataset of 330,387 citation-grounded question-answer (QA) pairs linking genetic mutations to their functional consequences as described in the biomedical literature. Each record pairs a protein-coding mutation with a natural-language question and an evidence-backed answer anchored to sentences in one of 27,442 open-access PubMed Central articles, spanning 6,620 genes and 125,593 gene-variant pairs. The dataset is constructed using CrossValQA, a framework that enforces information isolation between independent LLMs: one model generates QA pairs from an article, a second model answers the same question without access to the first model's response, and a third model judges whether each model's rationale supports the other's answer, so that retained QA pairs are reproducible from the source text rather than hallucinated. Of 401,406 audited QA pairs, 82.7% pass both directions of this cross-validation; those with a recoverable reference protein sequence form the released benchmark. In a 999-pair stratified audit, two expert annotators agree exactly on 86.4% of cross-validated QA pairs (95% CI 83.7-89.0; n = 638), a tier in which about 90% of ratings are "correct". Individual LLM judges agree with individual annotators at a comparable 87.0% on this tier but far less on QA pairs that fail cross-validation. Fine-tuning MutaPLM on MutQA nearly doubles its mean LLM-judge score for question-conditioned mutation-effect answering (1.45 to 2.82 on a 0-5 scale) and improves mutation-recovery accuracy from effect descriptions from 19.4% to 32.1%. Providing variant-matched MutQA retrieval context, without fine-tuning, improves strict answer accuracy across four LLM families by 20.0-28.6 percentage points, demonstrating the framework's ability to improve the reliability of LLM answers. We also apply CrossValQA to proteomics, providing a proof of concept for its use beyond mutation-specific QA. We release the dataset, construction framework, and evaluation code.

items.title: MedMLX: On-Device Medical Imaging AI for Apple Silicon
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Medical imaging research increasingly combines specialized artificial intelligence models for segmentation, detection, image synthesis and report generation. For three-dimensional CT and MRI, these workflows typically run on NVIDIA GPUs with substantial memory. On-device AI on widely available Apple Silicon computers could broaden access to these models for clinical researchers. These computers share a large memory pool between the CPU and GPU, which suits workflows that combine several models. However, few established imaging models run natively on Apple Silicon. Adapting a model to new hardware also requires verifying that its results match the original software. Methods: We developed MedMLX, a collection of 21 established medical imaging models rewritten for Apple Silicon in MLX, Apple's machine learning framework. The collection includes nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator, MedSAM2 and SAM 3. The models segment organs and tumors, detect lung nodules, generate synthetic images and draft radiology reports from CT, MRI, PET/CT, radiographs and endoscopic images. Using public cases from 11 imaging datasets, we compared the models' results with those of the original software run on an Intel CPU and an NVIDIA GPU. Agreement required a Dice coefficient of at least 0.99 for every segmentation label and equivalent criteria for other outputs. We measured memory use and processing time on an Apple M1 Max computer with 64 GB of memory. Results: MedMLX agreed with the original software in 211 of 212 comparisons. The single exception was a brain MRI segmentation. On this case, the original software itself gave different results on the two devices. We illustrated sequential workflows, including anatomical segmentation of a synthetic brain MRI and lesion synthesis guided by organ segmentation. With a memory-saving setting, 19 of the 21 models used less than 16 GB of memory. This setting reduced memory use by a median of 49% and increased processing time by a median of 13%. Conclusions: MedMLX enables on-device AI with established medical imaging models on Apple Silicon computers rather than specialized NVIDIA hardware. The models agree closely with the original software, and most need less than 16 GB of memory.

items.title: The Quagmire of Immunogenicity-Guided Antibody Design: Labels Limit Progress
items.abstract_or_text: Generative sequence-based antibody design is increasingly steered by learned property predictors, so a design objective is only as well specified as the labels behind its oracle. Immunogenicity is among the most clinically consequential properties to condition on, and among the least well specified: the supervisory signal is a single anti-drug-antibody percentage (ADA%) per molecule, aggregated from published trials. To analyze that signal, we first extended and corrected the widely used 217-entry dataset to 231 therapeutics with paired sequences, spanning formats from mouse to fully human. Then, we manually reconstructed the clinical evidence for 110 of them from primary sources. We find that an antibody format lookup outperforms every sequence-based learned predictor on the 231-antibody dataset. Apparent accuracy tracks the format composition of the evaluation split rather than sequence signal. Furthermore, the labels understate their own evidence: molecules labeled at [≤]6 ADA% span up to 86% across trials. We recomputed labels from the trial-level measurements and found that the advantage of the format-based approach disappears, while the sequence-based predictors degrade less under the cohort-weighted mean. We conclude that progress is limited by the label itself, and recommend reporting ADA% at the trial level, treating the target as a distribution rather than a point value, and evaluating against a format-based baseline.

items.title: Glutamine antagonism suppresses tumor growth in adrenocortical carcinoma through inhibition of de novo nucleotide biosynthesis
items.abstract_or_text: Dysregulation of cellular metabolism is a hallmark of cancer, which remains poorly understood in adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC). Here, we dissected ACC metabolism by integrating transcriptional profiling from human and mouse ACC, targeted tissue metabolomics from a mouse ACC model, and untargeted serum metabolomics from a large patient cohort, providing cross-species validation of metabolic rewiring in ACC. This study revealed global metabolic dysregulation, involving glutamine-dependent pathways such as amino-acid and hexosamine biosynthesis, nucleotide metabolism, and glutathione biosynthesis, suggesting glutamine catabolism is a critical metabolic vulnerability in ACC. Treatment with glutamine antagonists 6-Diazo-5-Oxo-L-Norleucine (DON) and JHU-083 elicited robust anti-tumor responses. Mechanistic studies revealed DON's anti-tumor effect was primarily driven by selective inhibition of glutamine-fueled de novo nucleotide biosynthesis. Additionally, DON led to DNA damage, which yielded potent synergism with inhibition of the DNA damage response pathway. Collectively, this work highlights glutamine metabolism as a central metabolic dependency and therapeutic target in ACC.

items.title: Digital pathological classification of peripheral neuroblastic tumors across multi-continent cohorts
items.abstract_or_text: Peripheral neuroblastic tumors (pNTs) are embryonal tumors of neural crest origin with highly variable clinical behaviors, ranging from spontaneous regression to aggressive and fatal disease. The International Neuroblastoma Pathology Classification (INPC) defines four diagnostic categories and stratifies tumors into Favorable Histology (FH) or Unfavorable Histology (UH) group based on age-linked assessment of tumor differentiation/maturation and the Mitosis-Karyorrhexis Index (MKI). Prognostic distinction according to INPC offers significant prediction of clinical outcomes, with patients harboring FH tumors demonstrating longer overall and event-free survival than those with UH tumor. Here, we assembled the largest multi-continental whole-slide histology imaging dataset of pNTs to date, comprising 2,030 tumors from the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Germany and Japan. Using this dataset, we developed NB-PathAssist, a computational pathology framework for automated INPC-based classification from digitized whole-slide images. NB-PathAssist integrates foundation-model-based feature extraction with an archetype-guided SummaryMixing architecture that compresses whole-slide morphology into representative histologic tokens for tumor-level classification. To automate MKI assessment, we manually annotated 14,049 nuclei, classifying them as mitotic-karyorrhectic (MK) tumor cells, non-MK tumor cells, or non-tumor cells. The resulting model was applied to phenotype cells in whole-slide images across 1,649 tissue sections. Across geographically and institutionally diverse cohorts, NB-PathAssist reproducibly assessed key diagnostic features and generated prognostic classifications concordant with reference INPC annotations. The average balanced accuracy for classifying tumor categories, grade of neuroblastic differentiation, MKI and prognostic groups achieved 0.84, 0.86, 0.89 and 0.96, respectively. We packaged the NB-PathAssist algorithms into an end-to-end online platform for scalable and standardized AI-assisted assessment of pNTs.

items.title: Single-nucleus transcriptomics links telencephalic cell signatures to ocean acidification effects on social behaviour in a coral reef fish
items.abstract_or_text: Mutualistic interactions are fundamental to the health and stability of reef ecosystems. While elevated CO2 has been implicated in impairments in interaction behaviours, how this environmental change alters cellular states and intercellular communication in the brain remains unresolved. Here, by analysing the single-nucleus RNA profile of ~66,000 telencephalic nuclei from a keystone mutualist, the cleaner wrasse ( Labroides dimidiatus ), interacting under ambient or elevated CO2 conditions, we identify highly cell type specific neural responses to elevated CO2. We highlight a substantial depletion in Oligodendrocyte Precursor Cells (OPCs), notably linked to oligodendrocyte myelination and neural structure maintenance. Elevated CO2 also elicited targeted transcriptional shifts across discrete cell types, characterised by widespread glutamatergic signalling and altered co-expression networks associated with pH regulation, energetic metabolism, and circadian rhythm, thereby compromising the cleaner's physiologic equilibrium. Additionally, cell-cell communication was altered under elevated CO2, including remodelling in SEMA4 and PTPR signalling pathways within radial glial and OPCs, respectively, revealing network signalling rewiring in response to the changed environment. These findings uncover the high-resolution neural substrates vulnerable to ocean acidification, providing mechanistic insight into how climate-driven environmental changes alter brain function and destabilise complex mutualistic ecological interactions.

items.title: CDC25B couples ribosome biogenesis to cell cycle kinetics to promote spinal cord neurogenesis
items.abstract_or_text: During neurogenesis, neural progenitors undergo a tightly regulated transition from proliferation to differentiation, which requires precise coordination between cell cycle progression and molecular reprogramming. Although the role of CDC25B is well established in promoting G2/M transition through CDK1 activation, we previously showed that it is both necessary and sufficient to trigger neural progenitor differentiation, via CDK-dependent and CDK-independent mechanisms. However, the molecular networks underlying this neurogenic activity remain poorly understood. Here, using a gain-of-function approach in the chicken spinal cord combined with bulk RNA sequencing, we show that CDC25B overexpression upregulates transcripts encoding ribosomal proteins and enhances ribosome biogenesis (RiBi) in neural progenitors. Consistent with these findings, during normal development, RiBi increases in neurogenic progenitor domains expressing CDC25B. Notably, the increase in RiBi is not associated with an increase in translation in neural progenitors. Instead, it is followed by an increase in mTORC1 activity in neuronal precursors and subsequently by a rise in the global translation rate in differentiating neurons. Moreover, increasing mTORC1 activity is sufficient to trigger a premature transition of neuronal precursors to the next step of differentiation. Altogether, our data support a model in which CDC25B coordinates cell cycle progression with RiBi in neurogenic progenitors, thereby initiating a program that culminates in translation in differentiating neurons.

items.title: Diabetic retinopathy feature utilisation in 54 convolutional neural networks: a heatmap analysis
items.abstract_or_text: Purpose: To investigate how artificial intelligence (AI) systems detect referable diabetic retinopathy (DR) from retinal photographs by analysing heatmap patterns and determining their overlap with DR features. Methods: Fifty-four AI systems were developed using 27 backbone architectures, with each implemented as both binary-referable and multi-class grading models based on the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy (ICDR) grading scale. Models were trained on DDR, BRSET and Kaggle datasets. After training, each model analysed 749 images with DR feature annotations, with Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients, LIME and SHAP heatmaps generated and compared to pixel-level annotations of microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots, venous beading, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities and neovascularisation. Results: All models achieved acceptable predictive performance (AUROC >0.8 for most architectures). Heatmap analysis revealed consistent attention to the central and temporal macular region. Exudates and cotton wool spots were highlighted most frequently by the heatmaps, with venous beading and neovascularisation at the disc showing poor overall coverage for binary referable classifiers. Models grading per the ICDR scale demonstrated higher coverage for all features. Substantial variability was observed between architectures, suggesting different feature detection capabilities. Interestingly, the heatmap analysis indicated that the models may be using different features to the ICDR grading scale definitions. Conclusion: AI models do not uniformly correlate with all DR features when detecting referable DR, limiting their predictive performance in unusual presentations. Heatmap aggregation analysis provides a scalable method for analysing model behaviour, allowing strengths and weaknesses to be assessed. These findings may help improve clinician's trust and acceptance of AI.

items.title: A regenerative stem cell phenotype marked by ANXA1 defines aggressive colorectal cancer biology
items.abstract_or_text: Background: LGR5 and ANXA1 are markers for specific intestinal stem cell states. LGR5+/ANXA1- crypt base columnar cells (CBCs) maintain homeostasis, whereas ANXA1+/LGR5- regenerative stem cells (RSCs) are present in fetal and repairing epithelium. Both states have been described in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet their clinical significance remains unclear. We aimed to determine how ANXA1 and LGR5 expression relates to molecular subtype, immune microenvironment and outcome in CRC. Methods: Dual-colour in situ hybridisation for ANXA1 and LGR5 was performed on tissue microarrays from 2163 patients in the randomised SCOT trial (ISRCTN59757862). AI-based digital pathology quantified marker-positive area by compartment and image based consensus molecular subtype (imCMS). Markers were related to clinicopathological, molecular and immune data, and to survival using Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox analyses. Results: ANXA1 and LGR5 showed inverse enrichment among a diverse group of parameters. ANXA1 was highest in CMS1 and LGR5 in CMS2, with CMS3 and CMS4 being intermediate. ANXA1 dominance was associated with right-sidedness, mismatch repair deficiency, BRAF-V600E mutation, high stromal content, T4 stage, low stromal FoxP3 and high epithelial CD68 density. Combining both markers improved prognostic discrimination compared with either alone (cancer-specific survival p<0.001; recurrence-free interval p=0.004), with ANXA1 dominance remaining an independent predictor of recurrence after adjustment (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.08-1.90, p=0.014). Conclusion: Relative ANXA1 enrichment defines an aggressive, stroma-rich, macrophage-enriched CRC subgroup with poor prognosis.

items.title: Perception and Challenges of Using Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Post Graduate Medical Education in Dar Es Salaam, Tanzania
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into healthcare and medical education, offering opportunities to enhance learning, teaching, and clinical decision-making. While AI has demonstrated considerable potential in medical training, evidence regarding its use in postgraduate medical education in low- and middle-income countries remains limited. This study explored the perceptions and challenges associated with AI use among postgraduate medical residents and faculty members in Tanzania and identified educational needs for its effective integration into training programs. Methods A descriptive qualitative study was conducted among postgraduate medical residents and faculty members from three universities offering postgraduate medical education in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. Participants were purposively selected to ensure representation across specialties and levels of training. Data were collected through four focus group discussions with residents and thirteen key informant interviews with faculty members. Audio-recorded interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed using conventional content analysis with the aid of MAXQDA version 24. The study was reported in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) guidelines. Results A total of 40 participants (27 residents and 13 faculty members) were included. Five major themes emerged from the analysis: (1) AI as a supportive learning tool that enhances understanding and educational efficiency; (2) concerns that excessive reliance on AI may undermine clinical reasoning and academic integrity; (3) limitations in the accuracy, reliability, and contextual relevance of AI-generated information; (4) barriers to effective AI use within the local context; and (5) the need for structured institutional support to guide safe and effective AI use. Participants reported that AI improved learning efficiency, facilitated access to information, simplified complex concepts, and enhanced teaching productivity. However, concerns were raised regarding overdependence on AI, reduced critical thinking, fabricated references, inconsistent outputs, and limited applicability of AI-generated recommendations to the Tanzanian healthcare context. Financial constraints, limited local data, and lack of formal AI training were identified as important barriers to effective AI utilization. Conclusions AI is perceived as a valuable adjunct to postgraduate medical education in Tanzania, with the potential to enhance learning and teaching practices. However, concerns regarding overreliance, information reliability, contextual applicability, and inadequate institutional guidance remain significant barriers to its effective use. Structured training, institutional policies, and equitable access to reliable AI platforms are essential to support the responsible integration of AI into postgraduate medical education.

items.title: Estimating glioblastoma migration-to-proliferation ratio from single time-point MRI data via radial density distribution
items.abstract_or_text: Glioblastoma (GBM) tumors with a high migration-to-proliferation ratio (D/k) are associated with treatment resistance, motivating the estimation of D/k from routine pre-treatment magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data and the investigation of mechanisms underlying its heterogeneity across patients. Unlike previous approaches based on nested spherical approximations of enhancing and non-enhancing tumor volumes, we incorporate the spatial arrangement of the enhancing and non-enhancing tumor regions by deriving a 1D tumor density distribution from their segmentations and fitting a 1D reaction-diffusion model to estimate D/k. We achieved an error of under 5% when comparing our method to synthetic density distributions and found excellent correlation with synthetic tumor segmentations (Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) = 0.996). We then evaluated associations between patient-specific D/k values and their clinical, transcriptomic, and radiomic features. When applied to 102 pre-treatment MRI scans from the Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) 2017 dataset, elevated D/k significantly correlated with reduced overall survival (log-rank p = 0.01), older age (p = 0.04), and a trend toward lower Karnofsky Performance Status (p = 0.059). In a subset of 91 patients with available microarray data, mesenchymal-like phenotypes consistently exhibited elevated D/k across three established molecular subtype classifications (p = 0.013, p = 0.055, and p = 0.127). Elastic Net regularization followed by overrepresentation analysis revealed an enrichment of glycosylation-related pathways among genes associated with D/k variability (p = 0.0123 and p = 0.0368). Furthermore, Multi-Omic Factor Analysis identified a radiomic factor correlated with D/k (r = 0.57, p = 4x10-9), with the highest-weighted features corresponding to smoothness of the non-enhancing tumor region on T2 and FLAIR.

items.title: Network analysis reveals converging molecular mechanisms in genetic epilepsies
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Rare genetic epilepsies are often difficult to diagnose and treat. They can arise from changes in many different genes, and the molecular basis linking these changes to epilepsy remains poorly understood. This complexity makes it difficult to select effective treatments and develop new therapies, leaving many patients with poorly controlled seizures and reduced quality of life Methods: To address this gap, we first identified epilepsy-associated genes and conducted a network-based analysis of biomolecular interactions in genetic epilepsy to identify converging pathways with high translational relevance and potential therapeutic targets. To run the analysis, we constructed a human brain-specific molecular interaction network by integrating all human pathways from the WikiPathways database. HotNet2 was then applied to identify highly perturbed clusters through evidence-based weight diffusion of EAGs in the human brain network. Results: We identified 2,496 epilepsy-associated genes (EAGs) from multiple resources. These genes encode coding for metabolite interconversion enzymes (20%), transporters (15%), and protein-modifying enzymes (11%). Furthermore, the network analysis identified 19 subnetworks with more than two nodes and 125 unique genes. Gene enrichment analysis revealed convergence of processes including action potential, synaptic function, nervous system development, TOR signaling, cilium organization, DNA repair, and cell fate specification. We identified 44 first-order neighbors connecting the subnetworks. By integrating drug-target interactions from DrugBank using CyTargetLinker, we highlighted potential therapeutic targets within the S4 subnetwork, associated with cerebral cortex development, as well as CREB1, a connector between subnetworks. Conclusion: Network analysis organized heterogeneous epilepsy-associated genes into biologically related subnetworks and generated hypotheses for further research.

items.title: Sex-based differences in fibrosis markers in human abdominal aortic aneurysms
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are a complex degenerative vascular disease. The role of fibrosis in AAA progression is unclear. Our study evaluated the impact of fibroblast activation protein (FAP), collagen, and vimentin on AAA fibrosis and progression. We hypothesized that FAP may influence fibrosis and disease severity in AAA, with potential sex-specific differences. Study Design: Multi-centered transcriptomic analysis of aortic samples from 15 human AAA and 5 non-AAA was performed to evaluate cell-specific fibrosis gene expression profiles. Histopathological and molecular analysis of 26 male and female AAA samples (mAAA and fAAA) and 29 male and female normal abdominal aortas (mNAA and fNAA) was performed to assess whole-tissue fibrosis markers and signaling. Results: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis identified eight major cell clusters with distinct sex-based distributions. Although vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) and fibroblast clusters had reduced counts in both male and female AAAs, they more highly expressed FAP and COL1A1 genes, particularly in females. Whole-tissue analysis demonstrated elevated extracellular matrix deposits with markedly increased collagen type 1 in both mAAA and fAAA. Alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA)-positive VSMCs were also reduced in mAAA and fAAA, but FAP was notably elevated, and robustly in fAAA. FAP-positive fibroblasts in fAAA exhibited increased expression of fibrosis markers, suggesting a unique pro-fibrotic phenotype. Conclusion: Our study reveals a sex-based difference in AAA tissue, with elevated fibrosis markers and increased FAP levels in females, suggesting its significant role in disease progression. These findings underscore the potential of FAP as a unique tissue biomarker for AAAs and warrants further investigation into novel targeted therapies that aim to stabilize AAAs, particularly in female patients.

items.title: Representation learning of somatic missense mutation landscapes across cancer types
items.abstract_or_text: Somatic missense mutations are pervasive in cancer genomes, yet existing studies have largely compressed them into mutation burden, mutation signatures, or driver gene annotations. Such representations obscure mutation-specific context and higher-order dependencies, leaving the latent biological structure of somatic mutation landscapes insufficiently characterized by systematic, data-driven approaches. Here we present MMRL, a pan-cancer Missense Mutation Representation Learning framework that learns the representations directly from somatic missense mutation profiles. By integrating mutation-associated features including gene identity, trinucleotide context, AlphaMissense pathogenicity, amino acid substitution and protein positional information, MMRL uses self-supervised learning to capture higher-order patterns among missense mutations across ~50,000 tumor samples from diverse cancer types. Across three pan-cancer cohorts, MMRL embeddings consistently achieved higher cross-validated prognostic discrimination than TMB and remained significantly associated with overall survival after adjustment for cancer type and TMB, as well as age where available. This prognostic value was also observed among patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors. Unsupervised clustering analysis of MMRL embeddings identified nine mutation subtypes in the TCGA pan-cancer cohort, with distinct survival outcomes, cancer-type compositions and mutational signature profiles, indicating that the learned embedding space captured clinically and biologically meaningful structure. Attention-based analyses further indicated that MMRL captured context-dependent mutation patterns beyond mutation frequency and predicted pathogenicity. Together, MMRL provides a data-driven strategy for decoding somatic missense mutation landscape and may facilitate precision oncology.
